title: Trace Fossils: The Stories Ancient Animals Left in Stone
summary:
When you hear 'fossil,' you might think of a dinosaur skeleton. But there's a second type: trace fossils. These preserve the activities of ancient life—footprints, burrows, nests, and even poop and vomit. While body fossils show what organisms were, trace fossils show what they did.

Both types form when remains or marks are left in sediment that later turns to rock. But trace fossils offer unique snapshots of daily life. Ichnologists—scientists who study these traces—can deduce diets, behaviors, and even speeds.

Take coprolites, or fossilized poop. They've revealed that pterosaurs ate mollusks and crustaceans over 150 million years ago. Fossilized stomach contents, called cololites, and fossil vomit, or regurgitalites, also provide dietary clues. One study found that Ice Age squirrels may have eaten woolly mammoth and wolf remains.

Burrows can show predatory behavior. Rocks from coastal Taiwan contain burrows likely dug by giant worms 20 million years ago. These suggest the worms lurked beneath the seafloor and shot out to ambush prey, similar to modern bobbit worms.

Dinosaur footprints in wet ground have helped scientists estimate running speeds. So trace fossils are like a detective kit for paleontologists, revealing the behavior of creatures that vanished millions of years ago. They remind us that every mark left in mud can become a story in stone.
why_it_matters: Trace fossils turn behaviour — eating, hunting, walking, burrowing — into evidence, which is something bones alone can rarely provide, so they reshape what scientists can claim about extinct life. The same logic now underpins the search for past life on other planets, where rovers hunt for traces and chemical signatures rather than skeletons.

background_read: Fossils come in two broad families: body fossils, which are the remains of an organism itself, and trace fossils — also called ichnofossils — which record what an organism did. Both form when remains or marks are buried in sediment that later hardens into rock.

The study of traces grew out of the work of early fossil hunters such as Mary Anning, a working-class English collector who pulled sea-reptile skeletons from the cliffs at Lyme Regis and noticed strange stony lumps inside them. William Buckland, an Oxford geologist, later named those lumps 'coprolites' and realised they were fossil dung, turning them into hard evidence about ancient diets.

Some traces are spectacular: the Laetoli footprints in Tanzania preserve the steps of early human ancestors walking upright, and dinosaur trackways have been used to work out how quickly large animals moved.

Because traces capture behaviour rather than bone shapes, they also matter far beyond Earth — space missions searching for signs of ancient microbial life on Mars look for chemical or physical traces, not skeletons.

perspectives.description: Trace fossils give researchers something body fossils almost never do: direct evidence of action. A coprolite proves a meal, a trackway records a stride, and a burrow shows an ambush strategy, letting scientists reconstruct ecosystems rather than just list species.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — hard to attribute and easy to lose
perspectives.description: A footprint rarely comes with a name tag, so matching a trace to the animal that made it is often guesswork, and identical marks can be produced by very different creatures. Trace fossils are also fragile: exposed trackways and burrows erode away, and without careful protection the evidence disappears before it is studied.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical — a young science with deep roots
perspectives.description: Ichnology developed alongside, and often in the shadow of, body-fossil hunting, and it only became a recognised field once researchers accepted that behaviour itself could be fossilised. The pattern is familiar in science: a category dismissed as unimportant later becomes a major source of evidence.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — from quarries to other planets
perspectives.description: New scanning and chemical techniques let scientists extract more from the same rocks, including traces of soft-bodied animals that left no skeleton at all. The same approach is being aimed at Mars, where rovers look for chemical or physical traces of ancient microbial life — meaning ichnology's detective work may one day be done on another world.
